rv.q: You can call the show brashly formulaic, sentimental or simplistic, but Newsies adheres to a time-honored Disney tradition of inspirational storytelling in the best possible sense.
Newsies” is Disney’s happiest outing since “The Lion King.
Disney has unveiled its finest fairy tale in over a decade, a fairy tale that, for once, doesn't concern royalty or implied-royalty or peasants aspiring to royalty.
The great asset of "Newsies," a show that should not be underestimated in its potential trajectory, is a demonstrable comfort in its own emotional skin and theatrical limitations.
It's a rare thrill to watch so many of them dance and jump en masse, and to hear them sing anthemic chants in unison.
There's not much news in "Newsies," but its most appealing headlines are selling hunks and hope.
Unfortunately, that is not the same as being exciting.

Newsies, which opened Thursday night on Broadway, is great fun, a rock-'em sock-'em American musical with all the trimmings, and an electrifying display that says, yes, formulas make sense when real artists make them work.
Like Oliver! and Annie before it, Newsies delivers the news that on Broadway, orphans can be irresistible.
The show has since been tweaked and polished to a dazzling family friendly delight; and if not "King Of New York," I have to say it's loaded with some very appealing princes.
Jeff Calhoun's excellent production benefits from a three-story set design of scaffolds, complimented by cinematic projections, and Christopher Gattelli's spectacular choreography.
“Newsies” gets syrupy faster than I hoped for and while never less than assured, its efforts to earn applause can come mighty close to pandering.
An exhilaring jolt of youthful energy has hit Broadway.

Newsies' contrivances are served with a light, knowing touch, and made even more palatable by the easy infectiousness of Alan Menken and Jack Feldman's songs and the youthful exuberance of the cast, under Jeff Calhoun's sprightly direction.
Newsies the Musical -- based on the so-so 1992 movie about striking newsboys -- is a slick, entertaining show that's sort of like Annie meets Billy Elliot.
But unlike his earlier hits, this production never really succeeds in carrying us to the height of emotion.
At a time when trade unions are beaten down by the big-money people who run our country, it is thrilling to see a play that celebrates the struggle of workers to get decent pay.
The choreography by Christopher Gattelli is dazzling.
A cult Disney movie gets re-crafted as an appealing family musical.

cn.t: Critics praise this energetic Disney musical as a crowd-pleasing triumph that rebounds from the studio's recent Broadway flops, though a few find the score generic. The dazzling choreography and youthful spirit win over most reviewers.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Nederlander Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here. Note: Nederlander Theatre itself warns of limited legroom in some orchestra rows.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out. As with the rest of the orchestra here, legroom can be tight in some rows.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well. As with the rest of the orchestra here, legroom can be tight in some rows.
A noticeable side angle, but Nederlander Theatre's more moderate size keeps the distance from the stage manageable.

vs.sum: An older theater in need of renovation, with virtually no rake in the orchestra — a tall person seated in front will block your view. First mezzanine row has a horizontal safety bar that partially obstructs sightlines. Legroom is tight throughout.

acc.note: Step-free main entrance to Orchestra. 6 wheelchair spaces. Personal induction loop devices available.
